blocks.content: DNS problems in a Kubernetes cluster trace back to a small number of recurring causes, most connecting directly to the Cluster DNS and CoreDNS topics covered in the Networking module.

This is exactly the real operational risk flagged directly in the Cluster DNS topic, if the CoreDNS Pods themselves become unhealthy, name-based service discovery breaks across the entire cluster, not just one application.

blocks.alt: The exact operational risk flagged explicitly in the Cluster DNS topic

blocks.content: 2. A Short Name Used Across Namespaces
blocks.text: 2. A Short Name Used Across Namespaces

blocks.content: Exactly the naming scheme covered in the Services module's DNS topic, a plain short name like my-service only resolves correctly within the same namespace, using it to reach a Service in a different namespace, without the namespace qualifier, simply fails.

blocks.alt: The exact naming scheme limitation covered in the DNS topic, now seen as a real failure

blocks.content: This is a real, easy-to-miss gotcha, a NetworkPolicy, covered in the Networking module, restricting a Pod's egress traffic too aggressively can accidentally block its DNS queries themselves, breaking name resolution as an unintended side effect.

blocks.alt: An unintended side effect of an overly broad egress restriction

blocks.content: The fastest way to confirm a genuine DNS problem is testing it directly, kubectl exec into any Pod and run nslookup or dig against the Service name in question, isolating whether the problem is genuinely DNS, or something else entirely.

blocks.alt: A direct test, isolating whether DNS is genuinely the actual problem

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: Unhealthy CoreDNS Pods, cross-namespace short names, and an overly restrictive NetworkPolicy blocking DNS traffic are the most common real DNS issues.
Testing directly with nslookup or dig from inside a Pod is the fastest way to confirm whether DNS is genuinely the actual problem before investigating further.
